questions.title: Question 1 — ABK Bank financial analysis
questions.scenario:
You have been provided with financial information for ABK Bank in the appendices. You are required to use this information to answer the questions that follow.

ABK Bank is a mature South African bank that has been operational for more than 100 years. It has recently been facing a number of challenges including the need to digitalize its operations as a response to increasing demand for online services from its customers, responding to new entrants in the market who are more agile thanks to embracing virtual banking and, most recently, the impact of the Covid pandemic on the banking sector.

You have been tasked with providing a full financial analysis of ABK bank using the information provided. Your responses to the questions should be framed in the context of the above description of the bank. Do not re-calculate any of the ratios already provided in Appendix 3.

parts.required: Provide an analysis of ABK bank's performance over the period under review (2017 to 2020). Your discussion should focus on the trends in the bank's Net Interest Margin and Return on Equity.
parts.memo:
Lecturer's comments: Firstly, let me emphasize again that this question provided you with all the necessary calculations and you were expressly asked not to re-calculate them. I highlighted that because I was worried that some of you might not read the whole question and end up wasting a lot of time doing calculations rather than answering the question. Unfortunately, many of you still did so and ended up with an answer that was 80% calculations and 20% discussion - only the discussion part carried marks. What would have been useful if you wanted to do it was to calculate growth rates to better indicate the changes in trends and assist in your interpretation.

The question was designed to give you an opportunity to show your understanding of bank financials beyond just the surface interpretations that have been the case so far. To that end, I tried to flesh out the financials by including breakdowns of the investments assets, operating expenses and so on. Those of you who scored well on this question, took your analysis a step further by drilling down into this additional information.

Many of you focused on just the basic analysis and that was fine - but your mark would have reflected this. Some of you broke your explanation down year-by-year rather than focusing on the shifting trends as a whole. For example, looking at NIM, you'd have three paragraphs discussing 2017 to 2018, 2018 to 2019, and 2019 to 2020. Unfortunately, when you did so, your discussion was generally just how the ratio changed from year to year without delving into the reasons for the change or how the overall trend changed from 2017 to 2020 and what that implied. This didn't really allow you to provide much insight and so even though you'd written a large block of text, you weren't providing much analysis besides what went up and what went down.

The ideal response focused on a couple of things - you discussed the trend in each of the key ratios (NIM, ROE, ASSET UTILIZATION, PROFIT MARGIN, LEVERAGE), you explained what was driving those trends and then you contextualized those trends given the bank's situation (increased competition, digitalization and the COVID-19 pandemic).

NIM has declined consistently over time from a high of 3,25% in 2017 to a low of 2,63% in 2020. Given that NIM is driven by Net Interest Income and TIEA, the change would be as a result of either or both of these variables. Looking at net interest income and expense, we see that both have declined consistently from 2018 to 2020. This might be a result of the increased competition the bank has been facing in recent years which has placed pressure on its margins. The decline has been the biggest in the most recent period though and this may reflect the competitive forces we've already mentioned but is more likely a function of the Reserve Bank reducing the repo rate by 3% over the period due to the pandemic. We know that lower interest rates in the market make it tougher for banks to have wider margins and this would therefore negatively impact the spread between interest income and interest expense.

On the asset side, earning assets have consistently risen from 2017 to 2021. From a simple perspective, a declining NII and an increasing EA figure would result in the declining NIM we've seen. Obviously, this implies that the bank's earning assets are not earning as efficiently as they once did. This may be a function of the mix of earning assets it has chosen over time. What stands out in 2020 is the large increase in derivative assets. Note that this was shown in the breakdown as separate from financial investments, so it's more likely that these were being used for hedging purposes rather than primarily as investments for earning purposes. It would then make sense that these would not be earning substantial returns and the bank would be utilizing them more to offset risk during the difficult pandemic period.

Looking at the breakdown of the financial assets line item in the balance sheet, we observe that more money has been moved into government bonds in 2020. This is another indication that the bank's investment mix moved slightly more towards lower risk investments in the most recent period due to the higher risk during the pandemic. It's therefore not surprising from this perspective that NIM might have decreased as a result.

Turning to ROE, we see the bank maintaining a fairly healthy ROE (above 16%) in 2017 and 2018 but a small decline in 2019 and then a significant drop in 2020 of more than half. The question is what is driving this change and the answer would be one or more of asset utilization, profit margin or leverage.

Looking at asset utilization, we know that the drivers are total income (NII+NIR) over total assets. Like the ROE, this measure has declined consistently over time, with its biggest drop again occurring in 2020. We know that assets have increased consistently every year from 2017 to 2020, mostly in the earning assets. On the other hand, we also know that NII has decreased over time for the reasons we spoke about before. What has happened with the NIR? The answer is that it was growing annually up until 2020 at which time it dropped significantly. Why might this be? Likely because NIR is tied to ancillary services the bank offers and many people would have been transacting less and making less use of the bank's products and services due to financial difficulties as a result of the COVID pandemic. As a result, the bank's fees charged for such services would have come down. So, we have assets increasing and total income decreasing, resulting in a declining asset utilization ratio.

On the profit margin side, our breakdown is NPAT over total income. We know from the above that total income has declined. At the same time, looking at the information we've been given, NPT has been inconsistent in prior years and actually more than halved in 2020. The 2020 drop appears to be a combination of the lower total income and a credit impairment figure that has almost tripled. We've already discussed the declining NII and NIR so we'll focus on the credit impairment increase. Obviously, this makes sense as banks in 2020 were making significant impairments to their loans because of the financial impact the pandemic had on borrowers. Many people were simply unable to keep up with their loan repayments and banks were offering payment holidays and various other schemes in an attempt to assist, but the bottom line was a lot of previously good quality debt had suddenly gone bad thanks to the economic fallout of the pandemic.

Finally, looking at leverage, we see that the bank has historically maintained a very tight and consistent degree of leverage, but this did spike slightly in 2020. This is not a cause for concern as the change was quite small and would have been beneficial given that the bank is not, as yet, suffering losses. At the same time, the increase in leverage was not large enough to offset the far more material declines in asset utilization and profit margin.

Taking all of this together, the bank has some significant problems. While the worst of its performance in the most recent year can be excused due to the impact of the pandemic, the reality is that its ratios have been worsening steadily over time, even before COVID. The biggest driver of this is probably the impact of increased competition squeezing its margins and its need to be able to compete with the newer style of online bank that has become prominent in the last few years (Discovery and Tyme Bank) which speaks to its need to digitalize faster and more efficiently.

parts.required: Operating Expenses and Credit Impairments are a bank's primary costs. Discuss the trends in these two line items using an appropriate ratio for each from Appendix 3.
parts.memo:
The two ratios in question are obviously the cost-to-income ratio for Operating Expenses and Credit Loss ratio for credit impairments.

Looking at operating expenses, we clearly see an increasing trend in operating expenses over time. We've been told this is a mature bank so we would expect to see some economies of scale if things are under control. We know that a "good" cost-to-income ratio is 50% and most banks, especially in South Africa, sit at around the 55%-57% mark. ABK's cost-to-income ratio is above this and has actually mostly been increasing over time, reaching a high of 64,1% in 2020. This is well above the 50% benchmark we've cited. Why is this the case? If we look at the breakdown of operating expenses, we note two things. The first is that their staff costs make up the bulk of these expenses and we know that staff costs are tough to reduce without some kind of downsizing exercise which has a myriad of knock-on effects and is therefore not usually an option. The second-biggest expense is information technology. This is also the only expense that has actually increased in 2020 - all of the others had decreased. Importantly, we know that ABK needs to digitalize urgently in order to become more competitive in its product offerings and how it deals with clients. This increase in IT expenditure is likely for that purpose and therefore makes sense. So from a cost side, yes there has been a small increase in operating expenses in 2020 but it appears to be justified.

In terms of credit impairments, credit impairments have historically been very small as per the credit loss ratio figures over time. Note that for some reason when I was creating the figures in excel, the two negative signs appeared for 2018 and 2019. They were not meant to be there, but I rolled with it while marking so that did not impact your marks at all. The key point here would have been that a good band is 1% to 3% and ABK has remained within that band throughout the last few years, including 2020, despite the huge increase in credit impairments as a result of COVID. This speaks to the quality of their loans. Some of you said that this indicated that their loan quality was poor, but I would disagree. COVID was an outlier event. People who were otherwise financially secure before the pandemic, were suddenly left without jobs despite never having been high risk before. The fact that the impact on the bank was still so well within the "margin of safety" demonstrates just how safe their loan book was.

parts.required: Assess the bank's risk profile over the review period, again using two appropriate ratios from Appendix 3.
parts.memo:
The best risk measures to use here with the Liquidity Coverage Ratio (LCR) and CET1 Ratio. The LCR is a measure of the bank's short-term liquidity and should be above 1 to meet the Basel regs. From the table we see that the bank's LCR has been above 1 in all years and was in fact highest in 2020. This indicates the bank's strong short-term liquidity. The substantial increase in 2020 is likely both a prudent move from the bank to ensure there was a buffer against any further sudden shocks to the economy but also as an indicator of safety to the market regarding its risk. Note that this is despite the requirement being relaxed by the SARB to just 0,8 to make it easier for banks to be compliant during the pandemic.

For the CET1 ratio, ABK has maintained its ratio above 13% consistently over time. This is well in excess of the regulatory requirements. The bank therefore has a significant cushion in case of any significant losses it may suddenly suffer. The combination of these two measures shows that the bank has very low risk despite the continued impact of the COVID pandemic.

Some of you did also use the loans-to-deposits ratio here as a measure of risk and I did allocate you some marks if your explanation was reasonable. The issue with using LDR as a measure of risk is that it pre-supposes that where the bank goes below the 80%-90% recommended ratio, that it is increasing risk. i.e. that if it is moving money from loans into other financial investments, this must indicate greater risk. This is not necessarily the case here. We said in the discussion for Q1 that most increase in the financial investments line item was due to investments in Government Bonds which are low-risk investments and the bank appeared to be taking on more derivatives for hedging purposes. So, the lower LDR ratio may actually have been a deliberate move to decrease risk in 2020 rather than increase it.

parts.required: Consider the Price-to-Book ratio and Cost of Equity for the bank provided in Appendix 3. What do each of these metrics suggest about the bank's ability to create value over the period under review?
parts.memo:
Briefly, a price-to-book ratio above 1 typically suggests value creation. Similarly, an ROE > CoE also suggests value creation as the company is earning more than its shareholders require.

Looking at the figures provided, ABK's price-to-book ratio is above 1 in all years which suggests that the bank has been consistent in creating value over time. The concern is the fact that the ratio has been declining steadily over time, suggesting that this value creation has been diminishing steadily in recent years.

This is confirmed when we look at the ROE vs CoE. The bank's ROE has exceeded its CoE in 2017 and 2018 and only barely so in 2019. In 2020, however, it was well below, mainly due to the sharp decline in NPAT we observed earlier. This suggests that even though the price-to-book ratio in 2020 was above 1, the bank actually destroyed value and the ratio may just be market optimism about the bank's ability to bounce back post-pandemic.

parts.required:
During a recent presentation by the CFO of ABK Bank, she suggested that the bank expected a significant financial recovery in 2021 as the market bounced back from the impact of the pandemic. Their internal forecasts suggested the ROE next year would be 15%, their net income growth rate would be 6%, and their cost of equity would remain unchanged.

Based on the bank's forecasts, what is their target P/BV ratio for 2021? What does this suggest about their value-creation for 2021?
parts.memo:
The implied P/V ratio = (Next year's RoE - g) / (Cost of Equity - g)

Note that the 15% given in the question is already next year's figure and therefore you did not have to grow it by 6% as some of you did.

The implied P/V ratio = (15% - 6%) / (15.05% - 6%) = 0,947 (as printed in the lecturer's memo).

This is below 1 and the bank is therefore expected to destroy value in 2021 (and this is unsurprising really given the trends we observed in 1.4).

Supplement (from the compiled Q&A, not the lecturer's): the arithmetic slip: 9,00 / 9,05 = 0,994, not 0,947. The conclusion (below 1, so a small amount of value is destroyed because the forecast ROE of 15% is still just below the 15,05% cost of equity) is unchanged.

parts.required: Based on your analysis, what do you think were the three most important issues facing the bank going into 2021?
parts.memo:
Suggested answer (not an official memo): three issues, each with insight rather than three words. For example: (1) falling NIM and NII from competition and low interest rates (NIM down from 3,25% to 2,63%); (2) the urgent and costly need to digitalise to compete with agile virtual banks (Discovery, TymeBank), while the cost-to-income ratio is already 64,1%; (3) recovering from Covid: credit impairments almost tripled, fee income fell and ROE (6,7%) is below the cost of equity (15,05%).

Lecturer's comment: This question was pretty open. You could have listed anything here as long as it made sense and showed some insight. Simply bullet-pointing three words was not sufficient.

parts.required: Cash concentration is one of the ways banks assist companies with multiple subsidiaries to manage their cash. Briefly explain how this works. Your answer should provide an explanation of both physical and notional pooling and how they differ.
parts.memo:
Lecturer's comment: This is straight from your slides.

Supplement (from the compiled Q&A, not the lecturer's): Cash concentration means moving balances (credit and debit) from the many accounts of a group's subsidiaries into one central master account. This gives treasury control and visibility of the group's cash, lets surplus funds from one unit cover another's overdraft (internal funding is cheaper than external), maximises interest earned and reduces interest paid on negative balances.

Physical pooling (sweeping): the bank physically moves the money. At end of day, as part of its electronic closing, it sweeps each sub-account to zero and concentrates the net balance in the master account (slide example: sub-accounts -R250, +R300, +R150 and master R0 become sub-accounts R0 and master R200). Variants: one-way (credit balances swept, not returned), target balance (a small set balance left in each sub-account) and reverse sweep (funds returned next morning for daily operations). It works best with one bank; across banks and time zones true end-of-day zero balancing is hard. Some countries (e.g. China) tax intercompany loans and interest, so unnecessary sweeps should be avoided.

Notional pooling: no money moves. The bank simply nets the balances of the accounts it holds and calculates interest on the net amount, as if they were one account. The result is the same as sweeping, but regulators usually require a cross-guarantee: each participant is jointly and severally liable for the others' debit balances up to its own credit balance. In practice all accounts must be with the same bank in one jurisdiction.

Difference: physical pooling transfers funds (creating intercompany loans, with possible tax effects), while notional pooling is only an interest calculation. Notional pooling avoids transfers and suits cross-currency use but needs a single bank and legal guarantees. Firms often combine them: sweep by currency, then pool notionally to one global master account.

parts.required: Calculate and comment on the company's Cash Conversion Cycle.
parts.memo:
Lecturer's answer. Note that you could only calculate the CCC for 2020 as you need the average figures for AR, Inventory and AP as part of the calculations. So, for example, DSO would have been average AR divided by Credit Sales x 365 = 79,75. Similarly:

DSO  |  79,75
DPO  |  113,48
DIO  |  170,33
CCC  |  136,59

Clearly, the CCC is terribly long. The biggest culprit appears to be DIO as the DPO far exceeds the DSO which is a positive for the company.

Supplement (from the compiled Q&A, not the lecturer's): DSO = (6 636 + 7 762) / 2 = 7 199 / 32 950 x 365 = 79,75 days; DIO = (8 331 + 8 431) / 2 = 8 381 / 17 960 x 365 = 170,33 days; DPO = (6 382 + 4 786) / 2 = 5 584 / 17 960 x 365 = 113,48 days; CCC = DSO + DIO - DPO = 79,75 + 170,33 - 113,48 = 136,6 days. (The lecturer calls this the 2020 CCC; it uses the 2021 flows with the average of the 2020 and 2021 balances.)

parts.required: If TFG was able to reduce its DIO by 30 days, how much cash would it free up?
parts.memo:
Lecturer's answer. Cash freed up = Average Inventory - (Cost of Sales / 365) x new DIO = 8 381 - (17 960 / 365) x 140,33 = 1 476,16 (Rm).

Supplement (from the compiled Q&A, not the lecturer's): new DIO = 170,33 - 30 = 140,33 days; 8 381 - 6 905 = R1 476m (the same as 17 960 / 365 x 30).

parts.memo: Lecturer's answer. This was straight from the notes. All I wanted here was a discussion about the trade-off between too much inventory (holding costs, obsolescence, opportunity costs) versus too little inventory (stock outs, customers buying from competitors).
